summary: Instagram is carrying the channel: almost every Hindi video gets 100 to 1,400 views there, while YouTube Shorts mostly gets under 25 views. The best performers are relatable, everyday-device or robot questions (PIR motion sensor, robot avoiding walls, street light), and the ones people share and save are the ones that explain a 'hidden magic' of something they see daily. The one English video did well on YouTube (161 views) but never went to Instagram, and several near-duplicate topics (two smoke alarms, two IR sensors, two taps) split the audience without adding much.
winningPattern: Short Hindi video about a sensor hidden inside a familiar everyday object or robot behavior, opened with a curiosity question or a surprising claim ('X doesn't see you!', 'How does Y know...?'), written in Hinglish with a 🤔 emoji, posted mainly on Instagram Reels. Titles that flip an assumption (sensor doesn't 'see') or name a daily situation get the most views, shares and saves.
doMore: Lead with a surprising 'myth-flip' hook like 'Sensor doesn't see you!' since the PIR and robot videos got the most shares and saves
Pick everyday-life objects people meet daily (street light, lift, tap, door, phone) and name the sensor inside as the reveal
Add a clear save/share prompt at the end, e.g. 'Save this for your next project', as saves and shares are weak on most videos
Cross-post the English Arduino video to Instagram and test whether English titles can lift YouTube, where Hindi is nearly invisible
Make one topic once, then follow with a series angle (e.g. 'Sensors in your home, Part 2') instead of near-duplicate videos
stopDoing: Publishing near-duplicate topics (second smoke detector, second IR, two automatic taps) within days of each other
Generic 'How does X work' titles without a twist or surprise, like the TV remote and ultrasonic ones that flatlined
Judging YouTube with the same Hindi-only Hinglish titles that get almost no views there
